scenes.tts: A pond drop may hold cells from across life. Which question should we ask first? The cells drift together, but a useful key needs an order. We will follow one mystery cell and let each answer open the next path.

scenes.visual: Hook before title. A large animated pond drop fills most of the frame. Gold, blue, and teal cartoon cells drift inside it. A white question path grows from the drop. COLOR MAP for both films: Eukarya gold; Bacteria blue; Archaea teal; trait evidence white; limits and stop signs red. Keep the cells moving gently.

scenes.visual: Title only: 'The First Split'. The pond drop remains large behind the title, and its cells continue drifting.

scenes.tts: Start with what a light microscope can show about cell organization. A nucleus is a membrane-wrapped compartment holding the D N A. If the cell has one, it belongs in Eukarya. If it does not, the organism is a prokaryote. Its D N A sits in the cytoplasm.
scenes.caption: Start with what a light microscope can show about cell organization. A nucleus is a membrane-wrapped compartment holding the DNA. If the cell has one, it belongs in Eukarya. If it does not, the organism is a prokaryote. Its DNA sits in the cytoplasm.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the carried mystery cell. A gold nucleus settles around a DNA bar, then the view transforms to a nucleus-free cell with the DNA bar in its cytoplasm. A large fork labelled 'nucleus' opens beneath it. No molecular structures.
scenes.narration: Start with what a light microscope can show about cell organization. A nucleus is a membrane-wrapped compartment holding the DNA. If the cell has one, it belongs in Eukarya. If it does not, the organism is a prokaryote. Its DNA sits in the cytoplasm.

scenes.tts: Our mystery cell has no nucleus. That rules out Eukarya, but Bacteria and Archaea remain. Both domains are made up of prokaryotes. Most are single cells, though some grow in chains or filaments. Under a classroom microscope, members of these domains can look alike.
scenes.caption: Our mystery cell has no nucleus. That rules out Eukarya, but Bacteria and Archaea remain. Both domains are made up of prokaryotes. Most are single cells, though some grow in chains or filaments. Under a classroom microscope, members of these domains can look alike.
scenes.visual: The gold path closes without a 'rejected' label. The nucleus-free cell duplicates into a blue and teal cartoon with the same outline. Brief chains and filaments grow from ghost copies, then return to the paired cells. The microscope circle stays around both.
scenes.narration: Our mystery cell has no nucleus. That rules out Eukarya, but Bacteria and Archaea remain. Both domains are made up of prokaryotes. Most are single cells, though some grow in chains or filaments. Under a classroom microscope, members of these domains can look alike.

scenes.tts: Look at these nucleus-free cells. Their shapes and sizes appear similar. Can the microscope alone place one in Bacteria and the other in Archaea? Choose yes or no, and name the evidence you trust.
scenes.caption: Look at these nucleus-free cells. Their shapes and sizes appear similar. Can the microscope alone place one in Bacteria and the other in Archaea? Choose yes or no, and name the evidence you trust.
scenes.visual: Enlarge the blue and teal cells side by side inside one microscope field. Their outlines slowly rotate. Between them, show the question 'Can looks decide?' with YES and NO targets. Do not reveal a choice.
scenes.narration: Look at these nucleus-free cells. Their shapes and sizes appear similar. Can the microscope alone place one in Bacteria and the other in Archaea? Choose yes or no, and name the evidence you trust.

scenes.visual: Hold the same question and moving cells for thinking time. A small white progress arc advances without numbers. No answer appears.

scenes.tts: No. Appearance has reached its limit, so the key must change evidence. Ribosomal R N A offers one test. Every cell uses this molecule to build proteins. Its sequence patterns differ between Bacteria and Archaea.
scenes.caption: No. Appearance has reached its limit, so the key must change evidence. Ribosomal RNA offers one test. Every cell uses this molecule to build proteins. Its sequence patterns differ between Bacteria and Archaea.
scenes.visual: The microscope circle becomes a red stop gate labelled 'looks'. It slides aside as schematic ribosomal RNA strips enter. Mark every strip 'schematic'. Blue and teal symbol sequences align; differing positions pulse in their domain colors.
scenes.narration: No. Appearance has reached its limit, so the key must change evidence. Ribosomal RNA offers one test. Every cell uses this molecule to build proteins. Its sequence patterns differ between Bacteria and Archaea.

scenes.tts: Picture each sequence as a labelled strip, not a molecular structure. Matching positions line up while differences flash. Scientists compare these patterns to judge relatedness. Early comparisons separated methane-making microbes from typical bacteria. Where looks failed, the molecules still differed.

scenes.visual: Keep the aligned schematic strips centered and tall. Matching blocks lock together; several differing blocks glow blue or teal. The strips bend into two separate branch paths carrying the same two cartoon cells forward.

scenes.tts: Cell chemistry adds another route. Most bacteria have peptidoglycan in their walls. Archaeal walls have none. In a membrane lipid, a chemical link holds the fatty tails. Typical bacteria use ester links; typical archaea use ether links. No single sketch proves identity. Use the full pattern of evidence.
scenes.caption: Cell chemistry adds another route. Most bacteria have peptidoglycan in their walls. Archaeal walls have none. In a membrane lipid, a chemical link holds the fatty tails. scenes.visual: Transform the strips into labelled evidence blocks around the cells. Blue receives 'peptidoglycan' and 'typical ester links'. Teal receives 'no peptidoglycan' and 'typical ether links'. Show each membrane lipid as a plain head block with two tail bars joined by a labelled link, never bonds or atoms.
scenes.narration: Cell chemistry adds another route. Most bacteria have peptidoglycan in their walls. Archaeal walls have none. In a membrane lipid, a chemical link holds the fatty tails. scenes.tts: Now the mystery cell carries an archaeal sequence pattern, no peptidoglycan, and typical ether-linked membrane lipids. Together those traits support Archaea. A different pattern would support Bacteria. The gate opens only when the evidence supports the placement.
scenes.caption: Now the mystery cell carries an archaeal sequence pattern, no peptidoglycan, and typical ether-linked membrane lipids. Together those traits support Archaea. A different pattern would support Bacteria. The gate opens only when the evidence supports the placement.
scenes.visual: The teal mystery cell collects three white evidence blocks. They fit into a teal gate labelled 'Archaea', which opens. A blue alternative path remains visible but neutral, without 'wrong', 'only', or extinction imagery.
scenes.narration: Now the mystery cell carries an archaeal sequence pattern, no peptidoglycan, and typical ether-linked membrane lipids. Together those traits support Archaea. A different pattern would support Bacteria. The gate opens only when the evidence supports the placement.

scenes.tts: Place the domains on branches, not steps. Sequence comparisons show relatedness, not a ladder from simple to advanced. All branches share a root. The course drawing is simplified. Archaea and Eukarya are more closely related to each other than either is to Bacteria.
scenes.caption: Place the domains on branches, not steps. Sequence comparisons show relatedness, not a ladder from simple to advanced. All branches share a root. The course drawing is simplified. Archaea and Eukarya are more closely related to each other than either is to Bacteria.
scenes.visual: The decision path curves into a large schematic tree marked 'schematic'. Blue Bacteria sits on one side of the root; teal Archaea and gold Eukarya share a fork with each other. All tips end at the same height. A staircase outline fades before labels appear. Keep all branches alive and equally bright.
scenes.narration: Place the domains on branches, not steps. Sequence comparisons show relatedness, not a ladder from simple to advanced. All branches share a root. The course drawing is simplified. Archaea and Eukarya are more closely related to each other than either is to Bacteria.

scenes.tts: This path has a limit. It places an unknown in the course's domain scheme; it does not identify every species. Keep the method, not a picture of rank. Classify by ordered traits; where looks fail, use molecular evidence.

scenes.visual: The tree transforms back into the ordered decision path. A red stop marker appears at 'species', then the full path brightens from nucleus to molecular evidence. The final rule begins forming but does not become an end card yet.
